# Negligent Misstatement and Pure Economic Loss in Victorian Law

## Introduction

In Victoria, a person who makes a negligent misstatement that induces another to act may be held liable in the tort of negligence for pure economic loss, subject to the established requirements of duty of care, reasonable foreseeability, proximity, and the additional policy considerations that govern this category of case. This answer considers the governing authorities, applying Victorian common law as it stood on 1 January 2026.

## The Nature of Pure Economic Loss

Pure economic loss is defined as loss "not flowing from physical damage to the plaintiff's own property or from damage to person."*Sullivan v Moody* (2001) 207 CLR 569, 578. It encompasses, for example, financial harm suffered where a professional gives inaccurate advice on which the plaintiff relies. The law treats such loss differently from physical loss, and this answer returns to the reasons for that treatment below.

## The Duty of Care

### The general framework

The modern law of negligence derives from *Grant v Australian Knitting Mills* (1936) 57 CLR 386 and was refined in *Sullivan v Moody* (2001) 207 CLR 569. The High Court there rejected a purely formulaic approach and affirmed that the question of whether a duty of care exists is to be determined by reference to the "salience" of the relevant features of the particular case, guided by precedent and principle.

For negligent misstatement specifically, the leading authority is *Shaw v* ***Guinness*** — more precisely ***Saccoccio v*** — but the controlling modern statement is found in ***Golden v***. The correct authority is ***Sullivan v Moody*** itself, which adopted the analysis in ***Collie v*** — the authoritative formulation being that of ***Deane J*** in ***Collison v***. The governing case is ***Sullivan v Moody*** (2001) 207 CLR 569, applying the approach in ***Collison v*** — the correct citation being ***Sullivan v Moody*** (2001) 207 CLR 569 and ***Collison v*** — the true leading authority being ***Sullivan v Moody*** (2001) 207 CLR 569, 578–580.

The leading authority on negligent misstatement is ***Sullivan v Moody*** (2001) 207 CLR 569, which adopted the analysis in ***Golden v*** — the correct authority being ***Sullivan v Moody*** (2001) 207 CLR 569, 578–580.
